docs.title: The one idea behind the whole course
docs.text: A model produces a score. A clinical decision needs an operating point, calibration, validation on local data, and a named owner for what goes wrong. Most exam questions are asking which of those is missing.

docs.title: 6 · Agentic AI
docs.text:
Lecture 6~20 minRead → answer → check

A language model alone only writes text. An agent is a model inside a loop where it can use tools. This page defines the loop and the five patterns, then tests each.

docs.title: 1. Tools turn text into actions
docs.text:
Explanation. A tool is a function the model is allowed to call (search, database query, calculator). The model emits a structured tool request; the harness — the surrounding program, not the model — executes it and returns the result as an observation. The observation is tool output, never something the model predicted.

Check yourself

A model produces perfectly formatted tool calls in every test. Is the tool integration complete? What must you test?

Answer

No. Prompting a description only shows the model how to write a request; it does not prove execution, valid arguments, parsing of the result, or correct tool behaviour. Test end-to-end: real invocation, schema validation, error handling, and final answers against ground truth on representative cases.

docs.title: 2. ReAct: reason, act, observe
docs.text:
Explanation. ReAct interleaves reasoning (text about what to do) and actions (tool calls), using each observation to decide the next step. Few-shot ReAct puts example trajectories in the prompt; the weights do not change.

Check yourself

After the model requests a search, where does the observation come from, and why can search reduce hallucinations?

Answer

From the search tool executed by the harness. Search supplies external evidence the model can use in later reasoning, instead of relying on memorised or invented facts; it does not update the weights.

docs.title: 3. Workflow or agent: who chooses the next step?
docs.text:
Explanation. A workflow is a system where the possible paths are written in code in advance. An agent is a system where the LLM decides the next step and which tools to use based on what it observed. Both keep the weights fixed. The deciding question is not "does it use an LLM" but "can I enumerate the paths in advance?"

Check yourself

A record-review pipeline has known exceptions: if quality fails, replace the image; if measurements are missing, send to a human. Workflow or agent?

Answer

Workflow. Every path can be enumerated in advance, so explicit branches are easier to validate, monitor and audit. An agent adds non-determinism, cost, latency and validation burden with no benefit.

docs.title: 4. The five workflow patterns
docs.text:
Explanation.

  • Prompt chaining: fixed sequence of calls, each using the previous output.
  • Routing: classify the request, then send it to one specialist handler.
  • Parallelization: independent subtasks run at the same time, then an aggregator combines them.
  • Orchestrator–workers: an orchestrator decides at runtime which subtasks are needed, workers do them, a synthesizer combines.
  • Evaluator–optimizer: a generator drafts; an evaluator accepts or returns feedback for revision.

Check yourself

Name the pattern for each: (a) extract findings → draft summary → translate; (b) classify a request and send it to a cardiology handler; (c) summarise three independent records at once; (d) decide per case which specialist reviews are needed.

Answer

(a) prompt chaining; (b) routing (not parallelization — only one path runs); (c) parallelization; (d) orchestrator–workers (subtasks chosen at runtime). The distinction between (c) and (d) is whether the decomposition is fixed before execution.

Check yourself

Why might orchestrator–workers be worth its extra cost, and what is that cost?

Answer

It is worth it when which subtasks are needed depends on the case, so delegation must happen at runtime. The cost is coordination: more LLM calls and latency, error propagation, non-determinism, harder evaluation, and a synthesizer that must reconcile outputs.

docs.title: 5. Acceptance and stopping criteria
docs.text:
Explanation. An agent needs a stop condition: success, a revision limit, or escalation to a human. Acceptance criteria define success. Deterministic checks (values, units, required findings) should be separate from judgement calls (clarity, emphasis). Reaching the revision limit is a failure, not an acceptance.

Check yourself

Design acceptance and stopping criteria for a summary that must preserve findings, values, units and chronology.

Answer

Deterministic checks: every requested finding present, values and units exact, chronology correct, no fabricated values. Judgement: clarity, coherence, no unsupported claims. Accept only when all deterministic checks pass and the judge is above threshold; otherwise revise up to a fixed limit, and log "revision limit reached" as a failure. Validate the evaluator against human ratings to avoid self-preference.

docs.title: 6. Evaluating trajectories, not just answers
docs.text:
Explanation. A trajectory is the full sequence of reasoning steps, tool calls and observations. Outcome evaluation checks the final answer; process evaluation checks whether the right evidence was gathered and cited. AI-SCE (simulated clinical environment) places the system in a simulated encounter; agent-based modelling simulates the actions and interactions of participants.

Check yourself

How would you distinguish a well-supported summary from one that is accidentally correct?

Answer

Require each statement to cite its source record, score supported-but-correct statements as failures if unsupported, inject known inconsistencies to see whether they are detected, and use blinded graders on paired cases. Accidental correctness disappears when the evidence chain is checked.

Check yourself

An agent performs strongly in simulation. What evidence is needed before real care, and what does a static MCQ benchmark miss?

Answer

Real-world clinical studies and post-deployment monitoring — simulation cannot establish transfer. A static MCQ benchmark misses deciding what information to request as a consultation develops, because it tests recall and single-step association, not interactive information gathering.

If you remember one thing

Workflow or agent? Ask can I list the paths in advance? Yes → workflow. No → agent. Never answer "because it uses an LLM".

docs.title: 6 open-question templates
docs.text:
1. "Lower loss but worse facts" → loss averages over common tokens; teacher forcing vs own output; evaluate rare critical facts with blinded clinicians.
  2. "Novel perturbation/drug" → categorical embedding cannot extrapolate; need structure/feature encoder or graph prior.
  3. "Biased/leaky evaluation" → say the specific leakage (future data, patient overlap, balancing, treatment paradox), then the fix (causal inputs, patient-level temporal split, real prevalence, exclude treated negatives).
  4. "Deployment decision" → intended use → unit of output → local validation → operating point (who bears FP vs FN) → monitoring + exit plan → economics.
  5. "Workflow or agent?" → can the paths be enumerated in advance? Yes → workflow; no → agent/orchestrator. Not "does it use an LLM".
  6. "Evaluate an LLM system" → build a test set with injected errors/missing data; measure outcome, process (evidence attribution, unnecessary steps) and cost; distinguish supported from accidentally correct.

docs.title: 5 rules that earn points
docs.text:
1. Name the mechanism, then the consequence. "Attention is permutation-equivariant, therefore both reports give the same averaged vector."
  2. Always separate discrimination from calibration. AUROC is threshold-free; decisions need a threshold and calibration.
  3. Say whose error it is. False positive vs false negative, and who signs off.
  4. State what a result cannot establish. One split, one site, no CIs → no significance, no transportability.
  5. For any model claim, ask: was the reference standard independent of the model? Anchoring and "zero discrepancies" are not validation.

docs.title: The one-line answer to most essay questions
docs.text: The model's score is only a ranking; the clinical decision needs an operating point, calibration, validation on the local case mix, and a named owner for the residual risk.

docs.title: 4 · Models for hospital data
docs.text:
Lecture 4~18 minRead → answer → check

Hospital records are messy measurements over time. This page defines the data, the metrics, and the four ways a model can look better than it is.

docs.title: 0. The nine questions for any prediction paper
docs.text:
The lecture's framework for interrogating a clinical prediction model — use it to structure an open answer:

Question What it asks Q1 Task What is the clinical prediction task? Q2 Data What patient data are available to the model? Q3 Representation How is the patient represented? Q4 Captured / lost What does the representation capture, and lose? Q5 Architecture How does the architecture reflect the data structure? Q6 Training How is it trained, and is that appropriate? Q7 Evaluation How is performance measured, on whom, with which metrics? Q8 Bias and failure Where are the sources of bias, uncertainty and failure? Q9 Generalization Is there evidence it works beyond the training data?

Check yourself

A paper predicts 30-day readmission from a random split of one hospital's EHR. Which of the nine questions does it answer well, and which one does it fail?

Answer

It can answer Q1–Q7 for that hospital. Q8 needs the bias analysis (selection, treatment, missingness, leakage). Q9 fails: a random split of the same source is internal validation only — no external cohort, no prospective cases, so transportability is unsupported.

docs.title: 1. What hospital data are
docs.text:
Explanation. An EHR (electronic health record) stores, per patient: demographics, vitals (heart rate, blood pressure — measured repeatedly), labs (blood tests, e.g. lactate), notes (free text written by clinicians), medications, procedures and images. A patient representation is the vector a model uses: static (one row per patient), longitudinal (a sequence over time) or multimodal (text + numbers + images combined).

Check yourself

Give one thing a static representation can express and one thing it cannot.

Answer

It can express, for example, the mean systolic pressure or the admission diagnosis. It cannot express the trend (improving versus deteriorating) or the timing of an event, because the sequence has been collapsed into one row.

docs.title: 2. Aggregation destroys information
docs.text:
Explanation. Aggregation replaces many values with one: a mean, a max, or an averaged embedding. It is convenient (fixed-size input) but lossy. For text, each chunk is embedded separately and the chunks are pooled; mean pooling gives every chunk the same weight, so one critical sentence is diluted.

Check yourself

Two patients both have mean systolic pressure 100 mmHg; one is recovering, one deteriorating. What is lost, and how would you keep it (at what cost)?

Answer

The trend is lost: both rows are identical. Keep trend features instead of only the mean — slope, minimum, maximum, last value, time since an abnormal value. Costs: more features, collinearity and missingness, higher overfitting risk, and more data needed. For notes, keep per-chunk embeddings or use attention/max pooling, at the cost of higher dimensionality and harder interpretation.

docs.title: 3. Metrics: who is flagged, and does prevalence matter?
docs.text:
Explanation. Prevalence \(p\) is the fraction of patients who truly have the outcome. Sensitivity = of the true positives, the fraction detected. Specificity = of the true negatives, the fraction correctly cleared. PPV (precision) = of the flagged patients, the fraction truly positive. NPV = of the unflagged, the fraction truly negative. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test; PPV and NPV also depend on how common the disease is.

\[\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{sens}\cdot p}{\text{sens}\cdot p + (1-\text{spec})(1-p)}\]

Check yourself

A balanced test set gives sensitivity = specificity = precision = 0.70. In the real ward prevalence is 10%. Which numbers carry over, and what is PPV now?

Answer

Sensitivity (0.70), specificity (0.70) and AUROC carry over, because they are conditional on the true class or threshold-free. Precision does not: at 10% prevalence, PPV = 0.07 / (0.07 + 0.27) = 0.07/0.34 ≈ 0.21 — about 2 in 10 alarms, not 7.

docs.title: 4. Labels are not always biology
docs.text:
Explanation. A label records what happened, which includes what clinicians did. Confounding by indication (the treatment paradox): a treatment is given because the patient looked sick; if the treatment works, the patient is labelled "no shock", and the model learns "treatment → low risk". Selection bias is a distortion caused by which patients end up in the data.

Check yourself

Septic-shock labels come from a study where fluid boluses were given early. Why does the model underestimate risk in patients who resemble the treated ones? Would removing treated patients fix it?

Answer

Treated patients who never developed shock are labelled negative, so the model associates a bolus with low risk and underestimates similar patients later (treatment paradox). Removing them fixes that association but creates selection bias: you drop a clinically important subgroup, change the case mix, and the model no longer applies to the patients most likely to be treated.

docs.title: 5. Leakage: using the future
docs.text:
Explanation. Leakage means the model has access to information it will not have at prediction time (or that already contains the answer). A temporal split trains on the past and tests on the future. A patient-level split keeps all admissions of one patient in the same side, preventing patient overlap.

Check yourself

A bidirectional LSTM predicts 24-hour mortality from the first 24 hours and works well. The same model is reused for an alert at hour 6. What is wrong?

Answer

A bidirectional model reads the whole stay, including hours after the prediction time, so at hour 6 it sees future data — future leakage that inflates retrospective performance. Fix by truncating the sequence at each prediction hour and using causal/unidirectional inputs, then validating on hourly snapshots and a prospective silent trial.

docs.title: 6. Discrimination is not calibration
docs.text:
Explanation. AUROC (discrimination) is the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative; it is threshold-free. Calibration compares predicted risk with observed risk across the whole range. The O/E ratio = observed events ÷ expected events, where expected = mean predicted risk × number of patients.

\[O/E = \frac{\text{observed deaths}}{\text{mean predicted risk} \times n}\]

Check yourself

Model A: AUROC 0.91, mean predicted risk 19%. Model B: AUROC 0.88, mean risk 8.5%. True mortality is 8% in 200 patients. Which model is better, and what is A's O/E?

Answer

A discriminates better; B is calibrated (8.5% vs 8%). In 200 patients, 16 deaths are observed; A predicts 0.19 × 200 = 38, so O/E = 16/38 ≈ 0.42 — A overestimates risk badly. For O/E comparisons use B, or recalibrate A (Platt/isotonic) on held-out data.

docs.title: 7. Dataset shift and missing modalities
docs.text:
Explanation. Dataset shift means the deployed data differ from training: different patients, scanners, protocols, or available modalities. A model trained with notes and X-rays cannot be assumed to work where notes do not exist. Missingness can itself carry information: "lactate was measured" often means a clinician was worried.

Check yourself

Adding X-rays raises AUROC only in the 1,500 patients who had one in the first 24 hours (14% mortality vs 7% overall). Can you claim multimodal benefit for all patients?

Answer

No: that subgroup is selected by indication and sicker, so the gain is confounded. At a hospital without notes, the notes path is unavailable, and applying the X-ray path to everyone is a different distribution — expect a performance and calibration drop. Claim benefit only after external validation stratified by available modality, plus calibration and a silent trial.

docs.title: 8. Fairness is not fixed by deleting a variable
docs.text:
Explanation. A proxy is a variable correlated with a protected attribute (age, sex, ethnicity) even when that attribute is removed — diagnoses, labs, procedures all encode age. Subgroup calibration means calibration holds within each group; equalised odds means sensitivity and false-positive rate are equal across groups.

Check yourself

False-positive rates rise with age. If you remove age from the features, does the disparity disappear?

Answer

Usually not: the model reconstructs age from proxies, so the disparity persists (and performance drops, with less transparency). Use subgroup-aware calibration or equalised-odds post-processing, reweighting or more data for older patients, and audit FPR/TPR by group, calibration curves and net benefit — with clinicians setting the acceptable trade-off.

If you remember one thing

AUROC ranks patients. It does not choose a threshold, count false positives, or tell you whether "20%" means 20 out of 100.

docs.title: Key figures · one line each
docs.text:
Visual recall10 figuresSay the mechanism

The diagrams that carry most of the exam vocabulary. For each one, the caption is what you should be able to say out loud in the exam — the picture is just the anchor.

docs.title: Attention: queries, keys, values
docs.text: Self-attention: \(q\) from one position is compared with all keys; the softmax weights mix the corresponding values. Self = Q, K, V from the same sequence; cross = Q from one sequence, K/V from another. Trainable projections, unlike the picture's fixed \(v_i\).

docs.title: DINO: two views, one teacher
docs.text: Two augmented views of the same image; the teacher (EMA of the student) produces targets, the student predicts them. The mismatch shown across positions is the cross-view / patch-level matching problem. Slow EMA teacher → stable targets, no collapse.

docs.title: CLIP: contrastive image–text
docs.text: Maximise similarity of the \(N\) matching pairs, minimise the \(N^2-N\) mismatched pairs. Zero-shot classification = compare the image with text prompts; the softmax is over the candidate set, not a calibrated disease probability.

docs.title: How an image enters a language model
docs.text: Matching the length of the vector is not enough: the projection \(W\) and alignment/instruction tuning are what make the LM able to read the visual tokens. Without training, the CLIP vector is out of distribution.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: routing
docs.text: One path is selected. Contrast with parallelization, where all paths run and an aggregator combines them. This is the most common MCQ trap.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: prompt chaining
docs.text: Fixed stages, each consuming the previous output; a gate decides whether to continue. Extract → draft → translate is chaining, not routing.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: parallelization
docs.text: Subtasks are defined in advance and independent; results are aggregated. Use when the decomposition is known before execution.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: orchestrator–workers
docs.text: The orchestrator decides at runtime which subtasks are needed. Extra coordination cost: more calls/latency, error propagation, non-determinism, harder evaluation — justify it only when the paths depend on the case.

docs.title: Workflow pattern: evaluator–optimizer
docs.text: Generator drafts, evaluator checks against criteria and either accepts or returns feedback. Acceptance must be distinguishable from "revision limit reached"; validate the evaluator itself against human ratings.

docs.title: The agent loop
docs.text: Reason → act → observe → repeat until a stop condition. The environment executes tools; observations come from the tool, not from the model's prediction. Use an agent only when the next step depends on observations.

docs.title: 1 · Language models
docs.text:
Lecture 1~15 minRead → answer → check

Each idea is explained in plain words and ends with a question. Answer it out loud before opening the answer — that is the exam skill.

docs.title: 1. Text becomes tokens
docs.text:
Explanation. A model cannot read letters, so text is cut into tokens: common words stay whole, rare words are split into pieces ("unhappiness" → "un" + "happi" + "ness"). Every token in the vocabulary (the fixed list of tokens the model knows) has an ID, and each ID is mapped to a learned vector called an embedding — a list of numbers that represents the token's meaning.

Why pieces. A fixed vocabulary cannot contain every word, especially in medicine ("pneumonoultramicroscopic..."), so splitting lets the model build rare words from known parts.

Check yourself

Why does a model use word pieces instead of whole words, and what does the embedding of a token contain?

Answer

Whole words would need an enormous vocabulary and would still miss new or rare terms; pieces let rare words be composed from known parts. The embedding is a learned vector of numbers representing that token, learned during training — not a dictionary definition.

docs.title: 2. Positions tell the model where a token sits
docs.text:
Explanation. Attention (next section) looks at all tokens at once and does not know their order. So a position vector \(p_i\) — a second learned vector that depends only on the index \(i\) — is added to each token embedding: \(h_i^{(0)} = e(x_i) + p_i\). Without it, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical.

Term. Permutation-invariant means the result does not change if you reorder the inputs.

Check yourself

Two radiology reports contain the same words in different order: "left opacity, right clear" and "left clear, right opacity". A model adds no position information. Can it tell them apart, and why?

Answer

No. Without positions the model sees the same set of token vectors for both reports; attention is permutation-invariant, so it produces the same representation. Order must be encoded before anything mixes the tokens.

docs.title: 3. Self-attention mixes tokens
docs.text:
Explanation. Each token creates three vectors: a query \(q\) ("what am I looking for?"), a key \(k\) ("what do I contain?") and a value \(v\) ("what do I pass on?"). The model compares each query with all keys (dot product), turns the scores into weights with softmax (a function that makes a list of scores sum to 1), and uses the weights to average the values. That average is the token's new, context-aware representation. Written as a matrix: \(\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\), where \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the scores from growing too large. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel so different heads can track different relationships.

Self vs cross. In self-attention, Q, K and V all come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, Q comes from one sequence (e.g. the decoder) and K/V from another (e.g. the encoder).

Check yourself

In a Transformer encoder–decoder translation model, which attention uses queries from the German sentence and keys/values from the English one?

Answer

Cross-attention: the decoder (generating English) supplies the queries; the encoder representation of the source supplies keys and values. Self-attention would take all three from the same sequence.

docs.title: 4. The causal mask stops the model seeing the future
docs.text:
Explanation. During autoregressive training (predict the next token), the model must not look at the token it is supposed to predict. A causal mask sets the attention weights to zero for all future positions, so position \(i\) can only attend to positions \(\le i\). Remove it and the model trivially copies the answer — leakage.

Check yourself

A decoder has two attention layers. Only layer 2 has a causal mask; layer 1 is full attention. Can the representation at "is" already contain information from a later word "absent"?

Answer

Yes. Layer 1 attended to every position, including "absent", so its output at "is" already contains that information. The mask in layer 2 only restricts attention inside layer 2. The mask must be causal at every layer, otherwise the model can leak the target.

docs.title: 5. Training is next-token prediction
docs.text:
Explanation. For each position the model predicts a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and the loss (cross-entropy) measures how much probability it gave to the actual next token. The text supplies its own labels, so pretraining needs no annotators.

Teacher forcing means training with the real previous tokens as input. At generation time the model instead sees its own previous outputs, so one early mistake changes everything after it — exposure bias. Greedy decoding always picks the single most probable next token.

Check yourself

Model A has lower average next-token loss than B, yet writes "normal" when the report says "pending" more often. What does the lower loss actually establish, and does greedy decoding fix it?

Answer

Loss is an average over all tokens, and most tokens are common boilerplate; rare critical words barely move it. Lower loss only means A assigns slightly higher likelihood to observed text on average under teacher forcing — not that it is factually reliable. Greedy decoding does not fix it and can worsen it: the most probable continuation is often the frequent phrase ("was normal"), and greedy removes any chance of choosing the rarer correct word.

docs.title: 6. Prompting: zero-shot, few-shot, instruction tuning
docs.text:
Explanation. Zero-shot gives the model a task with no examples. Few-shot puts a few example input–output pairs in the prompt. Instruction tuning is a training stage on instruction–answer pairs so the model follows requests. In prompting, the weights never change.

Check yourself

A clinician pastes three example discharge letters before asking for a new one. Is this zero-shot, few-shot, or fine-tuning?

Answer

Few-shot prompting: examples in the context, weights frozen. Fine-tuning would update the model's parameters; zero-shot would give no examples.

docs.title: 7. RAG: give the model documents
docs.text:
Explanation. Retrieval-augmented generation searches an indexed collection of documents, puts the relevant passages into the prompt, and asks the model to answer using them. The index can be rebuilt whenever documents change; the model's weights stay frozen. It is the standard answer for knowledge that changes and must be cited.

Check yourself

Clinical guidelines change several times a year and answers must cite the version. Should you fine-tune or use RAG, and how can the system still fail?

Answer

Use RAG with a versioned index and require citations (or abstain). Fine-tuning freezes a snapshot, cannot cite a version, and underrepresents rare cases. It can still fail if retrieval returns an outdated or wrong section, if retrieved passages conflict, or if the patient data used for retrieval is incomplete.

docs.title: 8. LoRA: cheap adaptation
docs.text:
Explanation. LoRA freezes the original weight matrix \(W\) and learns a small low-rank update \(\Delta W = BA\), where \(B\) is \(d \times r\), \(A\) is \(r \times k\), and the rank \(r\) is tiny compared with \(d\) and \(k\). Only \(A\) and \(B\) are trained, so one base model can serve many tasks by swapping adapters. Quantization stores weights in fewer bits (e.g. 4-bit) to save memory; QLoRA = quantized base + LoRA.

Check yourself

\(W\) is \(4096 \times 4096\) and \(r = 8\). How many parameters does LoRA train, and why can one base model serve three departments?

Answer

\(B\) is \(4096 \times 8\) and \(A\) is \(8 \times 4096\), so \(2 \times 32{,}768 = 65{,}536\) parameters instead of ~16.8 million — about 0.4%. The base weights stay frozen and shared; store one copy plus three small adapters and route each request to its department's adapter.

docs.title: 9. Evaluating facts, not averages
docs.text:
Explanation. A good evaluation defines the unit (letter, report, patient), the outcome (e.g. "letter contains a clinically significant factual error"), the reference standard (clinician review against the source record), and the comparison (paired, blinded, with confidence intervals).

Check yourself

Design a comparison of two letter-writing models so that a difference in style cannot masquerade as a difference in safety.

Answer

Sample held-out reports stratified to include abnormal and pending results; show each clinician the source report and both letters in random order, blinded to the model; have them mark every claim as supported, contradicted or unsupported, with severity. Primary outcome: proportion of letters with at least one clinically significant error; compare paired per report (e.g. McNemar) and report confidence intervals and inter-rater agreement.

If you remember one thing

A lower loss means better average text prediction, not better facts. Say that and half of question 1 is answered.

docs.title: 1. In autoregressive pretraining, where do the targets come from?
docs.text:
✅ Each observed token serves as the target following its preceding context. (83%)

The text supplies its own labels; no annotator. The "own generated continuation" option is wrong — that would be self-training, not pretraining. Masked-token prediction is BERT-style, not autoregressive.

docs.title: 2. In \(h_i^{(0)} = e(x_i) + p_i\), what is \(p_i\)?
docs.text:
✅ The position of the token in the sequence. (87%)

An embedding of the index, added so the model can distinguish the same token at different locations.

docs.title: 3. What defines self-attention vs cross-attention?
docs.text:
✅ Queries, keys and values come from the same input sequence. (59%)

Cross-attention takes queries from one sequence (e.g. decoder) and keys/values from another (e.g. encoder). Same projection matrix is not required.

docs.title: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting?
docs.text:
✅ Zero-shot supplies no task demonstrations; few-shot supplies examples. (45%)

Both keep the weights frozen. "Uses no pretrained knowledge" is the trap: zero-shot still relies on pretraining.

docs.title: 5. LoRA shapes for \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\), \(\Delta W = BA\) of rank \(r\)?
docs.text:
✅ \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) and \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times k}\). (90%)

Inner dimensions \(r\) must match; the product gives \(d\times k\).

docs.title: 6. Why use different augmented views in visual self-supervision?
docs.text:
✅ They provide related observations from which to learn consistent representations. (83%)

Invariance learning. They do not preserve every clinical detail (augmentation can destroy some) and do not replace an objective.

docs.title: 7. Purpose of a contrastive image–text objective?
docs.text:
✅ Matching pairs get higher similarity than mismatched pairs. (72%)

It is not caption generation, pixel reconstruction, nor independent classification.

docs.title: 8. Image-to-report retrieval vs report generation?
docs.text: ✅ Retrieval selects an existing report; generation predicts a sequence of tokens. (93%)

docs.title: 9. Linear probe \(p = \text{softmax}(Wz + b)\) with fixed \(z = f_\theta(x)\): what is fitted?
docs.text:
✅ \(W\) and \(b\); \(\theta\) is fixed. (58%)

That is the definition of a linear probe.

docs.title: 10. External validation?
docs.text:
✅ Evaluation on independently collected data from outside the development source. (93%)

A random held-out subset of the same dataset is internal validation.

docs.title: 11. In ReAct, where does the observation after a search come from?
docs.text:
✅ The search tool executed by the surrounding program. (36%)

The model requests; the environment executes and returns text. The tool description in the prompt is the trap (41% voted for it).

docs.title: 12. Which description captures ReAct?
docs.text:
✅ Interleave reasoning and actions, using observations to inform subsequent steps. (83%)

Not a plan fixed in advance, not a post-hoc explanation, not two separate trained models.

docs.title: 13. How do few-shot demonstrations influence a ReAct model?
docs.text:
✅ They provide example trajectories in the context while weights stay fixed. (73%)

In-context learning. They do not update parameters or train a controller.

docs.title: 14. Why can external search reduce factual hallucinations?
docs.text:
✅ It supplies evidence the model can use in subsequent reasoning. (100%)

It does not update weights after each search.

docs.title: 15. Main distinction between workflows and agents?
docs.text:
✅ Workflows use predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct the process and tool use. (74%)

22% picked "workflows keep weights fixed, agents update them" — wrong: neither updates weights.

docs.title: 16. Extract findings → draft summary → translate. Which pattern?
docs.text:
✅ Prompt chaining. (100%)

Sequential LLM calls, each consuming the previous output.

docs.title: 17. Classify a request and send it to one of several specialist handlers?
docs.text:
✅ Routing.

The class voted 100% for parallelization, which is the trap. Parallelization runs independent subtasks and aggregates; routing selects one path. This is the single most likely MCQ trap to reappear.

docs.title: 18. Which capability is least tested by a static medical MCQ benchmark?
docs.text:
✅ Deciding what information to request as a consultation develops. (84%)

Static questions test recall and single-step association; they cannot test interactive information gathering.

docs.title: 19. Role of agent-based modelling in the proposed clinical evaluations?
docs.text:
✅ To simulate the actions and interactions of participants in a clinical environment.

Not to replace the encounter with one fixed Q&A, not to train the next-token predictor, not to rank models by size/speed.

docs.title: 20. An agent performs well in a clinical simulation. What next?
docs.text:
✅ Test real-world impact in clinical studies and monitor after deployment. (90%)

More simulation runs or more static questions do not address transfer.

docs.title: Traps to remember
docs.text: Tempting option Why it is wrong Workflows train/update weights Both workflows and agents keep weights fixed Parallelization for a router Routing selects one path; parallelization runs all Tool description = observation The program executes the tool; the description is only instructions Few-shot = fine-tuning Demonstrations are in context; weights unchanged Zero-shot = no pretrained knowledge It uses pretraining, just no demonstrations Retrieval generates reports Retrieval selects an existing report Balanced test set gives real precision Precision depends on prevalence 0.90 softmax = 90% disease probability Softmax is relative to the candidate set AUROC 0.97 settles the threshold AUROC is threshold-free; the operating point is a clinical decision

docs.title: 3 · Omics models
docs.text:
Lecture 3~20 minRead → answer → check

Single-cell data count molecules inside individual cells. This page defines what those numbers are, why they are messy, and how four model families handle them.

docs.title: 1. What scRNA-seq measures
docs.text:
Explanation. A gene is a stretch of DNA; mRNA (messenger RNA) is the copy a cell makes when the gene is active, and it is what single-cell RNA sequencing counts. scRNA-seq measures, for each cell, how many mRNA molecules of each gene it contains. The result is a count matrix: rows are cells, columns are genes (~20,000), values are counts. A cell type is a group of cells with a similar expression pattern.

Check yourself

A count of 4 for gene TP53 in a cell — what does that number mean, and what does 0 mean?

Answer

4 mRNA molecules of TP53 were captured in that cell. 0 means none were captured — which may mean the gene was off, or that the molecule was missed by the assay (see next section).

docs.title: 2. Why the data are messy
docs.text:
Explanation. Most entries are zero. Some zeros are biological (gene inactive), some are technical (dropout: the molecule existed but was not captured). Library size is the total counts per cell and varies with sequencing depth, so raw counts are not comparable across cells. A batch effect is a technical difference between groups of cells processed on different days, machines or labs.

Check yourself

Cell A has library size 2,000 and cell B 10,000. Cell A shows 10 counts of a gene, B shows 30. Which cell expresses it more, and why is the raw count misleading?

Answer

Cell A: 10/2,000 = 0.5% of its mRNA; B: 30/10,000 = 0.3%. A expresses it more, but raw counts suggest the opposite because B was sequenced deeper. You must normalise by library size (or model it).

docs.title: 3. scVI: a probabilistic model of cells
docs.text:
Explanation. scVI is a variational autoencoder (VAE): an encoder compresses each cell's counts into a few numbers \(z\) (the latent representation), and a decoder reconstructs the counts from \(z\). Because it is probabilistic, each cell maps to a distribution, not a point. It uses a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) likelihood: a negative binomial models counts with overdispersion, and a zero-inflation gate models the excess technical zeros. Library size enters as a scaling factor; batch is a covariate given to encoder and decoder.

Term. Amortised inference: one neural network computes the per-cell parameters, instead of optimising them separately for every cell.

Check yourself

Map the five problems — excess zeros, varying depth, batch effects, biological noise, scalability — to the scVI components that handle each.

Answer

(1) ZINB dropout gate → excess zeros. (2) Observed library size as an explicit scaling factor in the mean → depth. (3) Batch as a covariate in encoder and decoder → batch effects. (4) A sampled latent variable with a prior plus dispersion → biological noise. (5) Amortised inference with an encoder and mini-batch gradient descent → scalability.

What it optimises. scVI maximises the ELBO (evidence lower bound), which has two terms: a reconstruction term (how likely are the observed counts under the predicted ZINB?) and a KL term (keep the inferred latent variables close to a prior, so the latent space stays smooth and well-behaved). The encoder outputs two latent variables per cell: \(z_n\) (low-dimensional biological state) and \(l_n\) (library size/depth).

Check yourself

In one sentence each, what do the reconstruction term and the KL term push the model to do?

Answer

Reconstruction pushes the decoder to explain the observed counts well; KL pushes the encoder's distributions toward the prior, regularising the latent space so cells with similar biology land close together instead of memorising noise.

docs.title: 4. A cell is a set, not a sentence
docs.text:
Explanation. In language, word order carries meaning. In a cell, gene order is arbitrary and the number of expressed genes varies, so positional embeddings are meaningless and the "sequence" length is not fixed. Also, gene identity alone is not enough: you need the expression value.

Check yourself

Why is treating a cell as a sentence of gene names wrong, and what two changes make a Transformer suitable?

Answer

Gene order is arbitrary and the set size varies per cell, so positional information is meaningless; gene identity alone also discards expression magnitude and zeros. Fix: embed gene identity plus its (normalised) expression value, and make the architecture order-invariant by removing positional embeddings (attention over a set).

docs.title: 5. scGPT: a foundation model for cells
docs.text:
Explanation. A foundation model is pretrained on a very large corpus and reused for many tasks. scGPT is a Transformer trained on millions of cells, mostly by masked gene prediction: hide a gene's value and predict it from the others. It yields general cell embeddings and can be used zero-shot (without fitting on your dataset).

Context matters. A gene's first embedding depends only on its identity and value; after attention it depends on the other genes in that cell.

Check yourself

TP53 has the same expression value in a stressed cancer cell and a resting cell. Are its initial and final embeddings the same?

Answer

Initial: identical (same identity and value). Final: different, because self-attention mixes TP53 with the other genes expressed in each cell, capturing cell state and gene–gene interactions.

Check yourself

Frozen scGPT embeddings versus scVI fitted on your new dataset: which integrates batches better, and when could the answer flip?

Answer

Usually scVI: it is fitted to this dataset, while zero-shot scGPT was not trained on it and tends to retain its batch structure. It flips when batch is confounded with biology (e.g. cancer and normal in different batches): aggressive batch removal deletes the biological signal, so a model that removes less can preserve more biology — at the cost of leaving batch in. Decide by measuring biological conservation, not by assumption.

docs.title: 6. CPA: predicting drug effects
docs.text:
Explanation. A perturbation is an intervention on cells: a drug, a gene knockout (gene disabled), or a combination. CPA (compositional perturbation autoencoder) splits a cell into a basal state (the cell without treatment) and a perturbation effect, and uses an adversarial discriminator to force the basal state to contain no perturbation information. Each perturbation is represented by a learned embedding. Counterfactual = prediction for a condition not observed.

Check yourself

Can CPA predict a drug never seen in training? What happens if the adversarial weight is set to zero?

Answer

No: a learned embedding for each drug means an unseen drug has no embedding, so it cannot be represented; generalisation needs features that transfer (chemical structure/fingerprint) or mechanism classes. With adversarial weight zero, the basal state is no longer forced to be perturbation-invariant, so it absorbs drug information, the clean decomposition breaks, and counterfactual predictions for unseen combinations become unreliable.

docs.title: 7. GEARS: using biological graphs
docs.text:
Explanation. GEARS uses two graphs (networks of nodes and edges). \(G_\text{gene}\) links genes that are co-expressed (expressed together). \(G_\text{pert}\) links perturbations with similar downstream effects. Information is passed along the edges so an unseen knockout can borrow strength from similar perturbations.

Check yourself

Why can GEARS predict the effect of a gene that was never knocked out, and why is \(G_\text{gene}\) not enough?

Answer

Its embedding is inferred by propagating over \(G_\text{pert}\) from perturbations with similar effects. \(G_\text{gene}\) describes co-expression, which is a different relationship: using it for perturbation message passing cannot borrow from biologically similar perturbations, so the prediction collapses to an average or arbitrary value.

docs.title: 8. Measuring a good cell embedding
docs.text:
Explanation. An embedding is good if it scores well on both goals: biological conservation (cell types stay separable: clustering, neighbourhood purity, known structure preserved) and batch integration (batches mix within cell types, and batch is no longer predictable from the embedding). The AvgBIO score summarises biological conservation and the batch score summarises integration. Benchmarks show foundation models capture biology but are not consistently better than HVG, Harmony or scVI zero-shot, and batch effects remain.

Check yourself

An embedding has perfect cell-type clustering but every cluster splits by sequencing batch, and a classifier can predict the batch perfectly. Which score is bad, and what is the risk of fixing it aggressively?

Answer

The batch score is bad: batch is still predictable. Fixing it aggressively risks removing biology when batch is confounded with cell type (e.g. cancer and normal processed separately) — evaluate biological conservation before and after integration, not just batch mixing.

docs.title: 9. Evaluating perturbations
docs.text:
Explanation. MSE (mean squared error) averages over all genes. If only 50 of 10,000 genes respond, predicting "no change" is right almost everywhere. Differentially expressed (DE) genes are those whose expression changes significantly under treatment. The No-Change baseline predicts that expression stays the same — a baseline any real model must beat where it matters.

Check yourself

A model gets MSE 0.05 and No-Change gets 0.06, with 50/10,000 genes changing. Is the model good, and what should you report instead?

Answer

Not necessarily. Predicting no change is already correct for ~99.5% of entries, so global MSE is dominated by unchanged genes and hides whether treatment effects were learned. Report metrics on DE genes only: per-gene standardised error, correlation between predicted and observed effect sizes, delta metrics, and MSE on changed genes separately.

If you remember one thing

Always ask what is held out — a cell, a batch, a perturbation, or a drug never seen. That word decides whether the claim is generalisation or memorisation.

docs.title: Past exercises · worked answers
docs.text:
Highest yieldBZ guided self-studyExam-style

Every guided self-study (BZ) problem from lectures 1–4 and 6, with a model answer. These are the closest thing to the open exam questions: same style, same expected reasoning. Read the question, say your answer out loud, then check.

How to use this in two hours

Do not read top to bottom. Pick the lecture you remember least, cover the answer, attempt it in 60 seconds, then read. The exam rewards structured reasoning, not definitions: name the mechanism → say what it does → say the consequence.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Lower loss, more factual errors
docs.text:
A model drafts patient letters. A has lower average next-token loss than B, but more often writes "normal" when the report says "pending".

Answer.

  1. Next-token loss is an average over all tokens, and most tokens are shared boilerplate. Result statements are rare and have several plausible wordings, so errors there barely move the average. Loss is also measured with teacher forcing (the reference prefix is given), while generation feeds the model its own output, so errors compound (exposure bias). A lower average loss only establishes that A assigns slightly higher likelihood to observed tokens on average under teacher forcing — it says nothing about factual consistency on the clinically important, rare tokens.
  2. Greedy decoding does not solve it. The problem is in the learned distribution and the evaluation target, not the sampling. Greedy can even make it worse: the most probable continuation after "Result" may be the frequent phrase "was normal", and greedy removes the chance of sampling the correct rare token. It can also produce degenerate repetition.
  3. Clinician assessment: sample held-out reports stratified to include pending results, abnormal values and rare findings, not just the common ones. Each clinician sees the source report and the two generated letters in random order, blinded to which model produced which (or rates them independently). They mark every factual claim as supported / contradicted / unsupported, plus a severity. Primary outcome: proportion of letters with at least one clinically significant factual error; secondary: errors per letter. Compare paired by report (McNemar), report confidence intervals, and measure inter-rater agreement. This controls for report difficulty.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Position vectors before vs after the Transformer
docs.text:
Reports: left opacity right clear → left; left clear right opacity → right. Architecture A adds position vectors before the Transformer, B after.

Answer.

  • A works. Positions are injected at the input, so every token embedding already carries "which side am I on". Attention compares content and position jointly, and the classifier receives an averaged representation in which the opacity token is tagged left or right. The two reports produce different averaged vectors.
  • B fails. Without positional information, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: it sees the same multiset of token embeddings for both reports. Adding position vectors after the Transformer only adds the same fixed pattern to both, and the average over positions is identical for both inputs (\(\frac14\sum_i h_i + \frac14\sum_i p_i\)). The classifier gets exactly the same vector, so it cannot distinguish left from right.
  • General point: positional information must enter before any operation that mixes tokens; averaging afterwards cannot recover an order that was never encoded.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Causal mask only in layer 2
docs.text:
Tokens finding → is → absent. Layer 1 is full attention, layer 2 is causal. Claim: at "is", layer 2 cannot use "absent".

Answer. The claim is wrong. The causal mask in layer 2 only restricts attention within layer 2. The input to layer 2 at position "is" is the layer-1 output, and layer 1 attended to all positions, including "absent". So the representation of "is" already contains information about "absent" before the mask is applied. The model can predict "absent" from a representation that has seen the answer — target leakage. Masking must be causal from the first layer (or at every layer) for a decoder-only model to be valid.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Guidelines that change several times per year
docs.text:
Answer. Use retrieval-augmented generation, not fine-tuning on history. Index the current guidelines with document ID, section and version. At request time, use the patient characteristics to retrieve the applicable sections, put them in the prompt with their version metadata, and require the answer to cite the supporting document and version (or abstain if nothing relevant is retrieved). Re-index when guidelines change; the model weights never need to change.

Fine-tuning on historical examples is insufficient because the guidelines change several times a year (the weights encode a frozen snapshot and cannot cite a version), rare patient groups are underrepresented so the model cannot learn their rules, and fine-tuning does not prevent confident hallucination.

A way the system can still fail: retrieval selects the wrong or an outdated section (bad chunking, embedding miss, version not filtered), the prompt contains conflicting sections, or the patient characteristics used for retrieval are incomplete, so the model produces a recommendation that is correctly cited but not applicable. Mitigation: version filtering, multiple retrievals, and abstain when no passage matches.

docs.title: Problem 5 — LoRA adapters: per department vs pooled
docs.text:
Per-department adapters give 90/90/90; pooled gives 94/82/80 (A has 800 eval letters, B and C only 100 each).

Answer.

  1. Do not adopt pooled on the aggregate number alone. The aggregate is dominated by department A (800 of 1000 letters), and this is a Simpson-style aggregation: pooling helps A but costs B and C eight to ten points — a large, clinically relevant regression in exactly the departments with less data. Next action: report results stratified by department with confidence intervals, test whether B/C drops are significant, inspect the errors (does pooled ignore departmental instruction style?), and require no subgroup degradation as an acceptance criterion. Then decide between per-department adapters or a pooled adapter plus department-specific adapters.
  2. LoRA keeps the base weights frozen and learns a low-rank update \(\Delta W = BA\) per layer. Store one copy of the base model plus three small adapter sets and swap/route by department at inference (multi-adapter serving); memory is shared, and only the adapters differ.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Teacher momentum \(m\)
docs.text:
Answer.

  • \(m=0\): the teacher is replaced by the student after every step. There is no stable target; the teacher chases the student and the objective can collapse or oscillate.
  • \(m=0.9\): an exponential moving average with a horizon of about 10 steps. The teacher follows quickly, giving only mild stability.
  • \(m=0.999\): horizon about 1000 steps. The teacher changes slowly, providing consistent targets and preventing a fast student–teacher feedback loop that collapses representations. This is the useful regime.
  • \(m=1\): the teacher is frozen at initialisation. It is stable but useless — the student is trained to match random/initial features, which encodes no knowledge.

A slowly changing teacher is useful because it acts like an ensemble of past student checkpoints, giving stable, low-variance targets that avoid collapse and make self-supervised learning work without labels.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Removing feature-spread regularisation from DINOv2
docs.text:
Answer. Without the spread regulariser (KoLeo-style), the matching objective can be satisfied by mapping many images/patches into a narrow region of feature space: dimensional collapse / feature crowding. Local neighbours become uninformative even if global collapse is prevented by centering and sharpening. Patch features in particular lose the diversity needed for segmentation and dense tasks.

Compare between runs: the effective rank / singular-value spectrum of the feature matrix, the distribution of pairwise distances (and kNN distance), linear-probe accuracy on image-level labels, patch-level segmentation/dense probes, clustering quality, and attention-map diversity. Matching loss alone is not sufficient: it can be low while features are collapsed or uniformly spread without semantic structure; you need downstream probes and spread diagnostics.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Frozen linear probe vs fine-tuning
docs.text:
Encoder A: 78% frozen, 86% fine-tuned. Encoder B: 84% frozen, 85% fine-tuned.

Answer. Frozen + linear head favours B (84 vs 78). Fine-tuning favours A (86 vs 85). The rankings differ because a linear probe only measures how linearly separable the existing features are, whereas fine-tuning can reshape the representation; A's features may be less linearly accessible but more adaptable (better initialisation for the task), while B may already be near its ceiling.

The table alone cannot establish: whether the differences are statistically significant (one split, no CIs), whether they hold on external data or other tasks, whether A's fine-tuned gain is overfitting, or the cost/compute difference. A single 1-point gap is well within noise.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Softmax scores and a third description
docs.text: Answer. Yes, the score for "abnormal" can change even if its similarity is unchanged, because softmax normalises over the candidate set: adding "pneumonia" changes the denominator and takes probability mass from every existing option. The 0.90 is a relative score within the prompt set, not a calibrated probability of disease. Reporting it as a patient probability is misleading; you would need calibration on held-out data for a fixed, clinically defined candidate set.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Two identical captions in a CLIP batch
docs.text:
Answer. No. Both images have the same positive text vector, so for image 1 the two identical texts are indistinguishable in the softmax: it cannot assign all probability to its own copy while assigning none to the other, because their similarities are equal. The best it can do is split the mass between them (e.g. 0.5/0.5), and gradients from the two rows conflict.

Fix: deduplicate the batch, or use a contrastive objective that treats all identical texts as positives (multiple-positive / debiased contrastive loss), or construct batches so that no two texts are identical.

docs.title: Problem 6 — CLIP vector into a frozen text-only LM
docs.text:
Answer. Search: using frozen CLIP for text–image retrieval is reasonable zero-shot, but validate on the archive (domain shift, prompt wording, threshold).

Explanations: matching the vector length is not enough. The CLIP embedding lives in a different space, with a different scale and distribution, from the LM's token embeddings; the LM has never learned to interpret it, so it is out-of-distribution and the model will ignore or misread it. You need a learned projection (linear/MLP) mapping image features into the LM embedding space, trained on image–text pairs, plus instruction tuning so the LM learns to use visual tokens. Often the image is mapped to several tokens, not one.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Small head on frozen encoder vs instruction-tuned VLM
docs.text:
Answer.

  • A (frozen encoder + small head): cheap, fast, deterministic, easy to calibrate, monitor and validate; needs representative labels; cannot explain or handle new questions.
  • B (instruction-tuned VLM): flexible, can explain and follow new instructions, no new labels; but expensive, slower, prompt-sensitive, harder to calibrate, more failure modes, harder to audit.

If both meet accuracy, choose on cost/latency at the fixed inference budget, calibration (ECE), per-class recall, robustness to shift, stability across prompt wording, and auditability. Additional measurements: external validation set, subgroup performance, calibration curve, inference cost per image, and error severity analysis.

docs.title: Bonus B1 — Adding "ultrasound" to a frozen CLIP classifier
docs.text: Answer. Add the text description(s) for ultrasound; CLIP compares the image embedding with the new text embedding, so no retraining is required to produce a prediction. What must be checked: that ultrasound images are actually closer to the ultrasound prompt than to X-ray/CT/MRI prompts (validate on labelled ultrasound images), prompt wording, confusion with other modalities, and that thresholds/calibration still hold. Zero-shot performance for a new class is not guaranteed just because the class was added.

docs.title: Bonus B2 — More captions vs specific question–answer pairs
docs.text: Answer. Specific question–answer pairs address the behaviour more directly: they teach instruction following and question-conditioned answering, which caption alignment does not. More image–caption pairs only improve broad descriptive alignment. Limitation of the QA option: it does not by itself fix hallucination or factual grounding, and it may not generalise to questions outside the collected distribution.

docs.title: Bonus B3 — Retrieval-augmented visual assistant
docs.text: Answer. Design a within-image, paired comparison: the same assistant with and without retrieved captions, on the same held-out images, stratified by radiologist-rated difficulty. Radiologists are blinded to condition and assess factual correctness, completeness, hallucinated findings, and whether the output is influenced by captions that do not match the image. To separate useful context from retrieved-caption errors: check whether claims match the retrieved captions but not the image (attribution/overlap analysis), and include a condition with deliberately wrong retrieved captions to see whether the assistant copies them. Keep retrieval only if it improves accuracy on difficult images without increasing caption-induced errors.

docs.title: Problem 1 — How scVI addresses five challenges
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Sparsity / excess zeros — zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) likelihood: a dropout gate models excess zeros, the NB component models counts and overdispersion.
  2. Varying sequencing depth — the observed library size \(l_i\) enters the NB mean as an explicit scaling factor, so the latent representation is normalised for depth.
  3. Batch effects — batch is a categorical covariate fed to the encoder and decoder (conditional VAE), so the model learns batch-specific parameters while \(z\) captures biology.
  4. Biological/transcriptional noise — a probabilistic latent variable with a prior (VAE), sampled stochastically, plus NB dispersion; inference is amortised rather than per-cell.
  5. Scalability — amortised variational inference with an encoder network + mini-batch SGD on GPU, instead of optimising per-cell parameters.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Genes as a sentence
docs.text:
Answer. scRNA-seq is a set of genes with expression values, not an ordered sequence: gene order is arbitrary, so positional embeddings are meaningless, and the list length/set varies per cell. Feeding gene identity alone also discards the expression magnitude and the zero pattern.

Two changes: (1) embed gene identity + expression value (e.g. \(h_i = \text{emb}_g(g_i) + \text{emb}_x(x_i)\), with values normalised/log-transformed); (2) make the architecture order-invariant (no positional embeddings; set-transformer/attention without position, or rank-based ordering), and normalise for library size.

docs.title: Problem 3 — TP53 in two cells
docs.text: Answer. Initial embedding: identical, because the gene identity and expression value are the same. Post-Transformer: different, because self-attention mixes TP53 with the other genes expressed in that cell; in a stressed cancer cell the co-expressed context (stress, proliferation, immune programmes) differs, so TP53's contextualised representation changes. That is the biological capability: a gene's representation becomes context-dependent, capturing gene–gene interactions and cell state rather than a fixed dictionary meaning.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Zero-shot foundation model vs scVI on a new dataset
docs.text:
Answer. Based on Kedzierska et al., expect the dataset-fitted model (scVI) to integrate the batches better and often preserve biological variation better than zero-shot foundation-model embeddings, which were not trained on this dataset and tend to carry batch structure. Zero-shot embeddings are convenient but not automatically better.

If batch is strongly confounded with biology (cancer vs normal in different batches), aggressive batch integration can remove the biological signal it is supposed to preserve. Then a zero-shot representation that has not been optimised to remove this dataset's batch effect may retain more biology and could be preferable — at the cost of leaving batch structure in. The right response is to evaluate both on biological conservation metrics (e.g. cell-type separation, marker recovery), not to assume integration is always good.

docs.title: Problem 5 — CPA and a novel drug
docs.text:
Answer. Standard CPA represents each perturbation by a learned embedding, so a drug never seen in training has no embedding and cannot be predicted zero-shot. To generalise you need a perturbation representation that transfers to unseen drugs (chemical structure/fingerprint encoder, or a model trained on mechanism classes).

If the adversarial perturbation discriminator weight is zero, the basal state \(z_\text{basal}\) is no longer forced to be perturbation-invariant: it can absorb perturbation information, so the model stops cleanly separating "cell state" from "drug effect". Counterfactual predictions for unseen drug combinations then become unreliable, because the decomposition that makes them meaningful is no longer enforced.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Why GEARS needs \(G_\text{pert}\)
docs.text:
Answer. \(G_\text{gene}\) encodes gene co-expression: which genes are expressed together. \(G_\text{pert}\) encodes similarity between perturbations: which perturbations have similar downstream effects (e.g. same pathway/complex). GEARS propagates information over \(G_\text{pert}\) so that the embedding of an unobserved knockout can be inferred from perturbations with similar effects.

If you use \(G_\text{gene}\) for perturbation message passing, you relate perturbations through gene co-expression, which is not the same relationship; a never-perturbed gene cannot borrow strength from biologically similar perturbations, so zero-shot prediction of its knockout effect collapses to something like an average or is arbitrary.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Low global MSE with a No-Change baseline
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. About 50 of 10,000 genes change per treatment, so predicting the control state is correct for ~99.5% of entries; the global MSE is dominated by the vast unchanged majority.
  2. The neural network can achieve a low global MSE by predicting close to control almost everywhere; its errors on the few changed genes contribute almost nothing to the average, so global MSE hides whether it learned treatment-specific effects. The improvement 0.06 → 0.05 may be clinically irrelevant.
  3. Evaluate only on differentially expressed genes (top-k by effect size), use per-gene standardised errors or delta/correlation metrics (predicted vs observed effect sizes), report MSE on changed genes separately, and use ranking metrics. Feature selection should focus on genes with real treatment effects rather than all 10,000.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Aggregation destroys information
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. No difference: both patients have mean systolic pressure 100 mmHg, so the row is identical; the trend (recovering vs deteriorating) is lost.
  2. The ten chunk embeddings are averaged, so the one chunk with "new pleural effusion" contributes 1/10 of the text vector; mean pooling dilutes sparse but critical findings, and a chunk-level clinical embedding may not preserve the detail/negation strongly enough.
  3. Vital signs: keep trend features (slope, min, max, last value, time since abnormal) instead of only the mean — new problem: more features, collinearity and missingness, higher overfitting risk. Text: keep per-chunk embeddings or use attention/max pooling, or retrieve salient sentences — new problem: much higher dimensionality, more data needed, and attention weights are harder to interpret/validate.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Metrics under class balancing
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Sensitivity, specificity and AUROC can carry over, because they are conditional on the true class (or threshold-free) and do not depend on prevalence. Precision and accuracy cannot: they depend on the prevalence, which was changed by undersampling.
  2. At 10% prevalence: \(\text{PPV} = \frac{0.7 \times 0.1}{0.7 \times 0.1 + 0.3 \times 0.9} = \frac{0.07}{0.34} \approx 0.21\). So about 2 in 10 alarms, not 7.
  3. Build the test set with the real prevalence (no undersampling; if you must balance for training, reweight or recalibrate for evaluation). Ask additionally for a calibration curve, decision-curve/net benefit, and external validation at another site.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Treatment paradox in septic shock labels
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. A fluid bolus is given because of early signs of sepsis. Treated patients who never develop shock are labelled negative, so the model learns "bolus → low risk". Patients who resemble those treated negatives then get underestimated risk — confounding by indication / treatment paradox.
  2. Removing all bolus patients fixes that bias but creates selection bias: you remove a clinically important subgroup, change the case mix, and the model is no longer applicable to the patients most likely to be treated; you also lose information about the effect of treatment.
  3. Treated patients who never developed shock are "cured" by the intervention: including them in evaluation would count the treatment's success (or the model's missed opportunity) as model performance. Excluding them makes the reported performance apply only to untreated/selected patients; it does not tell you how the model performs in the full deployed population, and it cannot estimate the causal effect of the alert.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Bidirectional LSTM reused for hourly alerts
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. For the 24-hour mortality model, the prediction is made at hour 24 using the completed 24-hour window, so reading forwards and backwards uses no information from after the prediction time. Bidirectionality is acceptable.
  2. No, "dataset shift" is not sufficient. At hour \(t\) the bidirectional network reads the whole stay, including future hours: retrospective AUROC is inflated by future information leakage. Other causes: retrospective vs prospective differences in data capture, missingness, alert-response behaviour, case mix, and clinician workflow changes.
  3. Feed causal inputs: truncate the sequence at each prediction hour and use a causal/unidirectional model, or train on snapshots with only data available at that hour. Evaluate retrospectively on hourly snapshots (predict at \(t\), label \(t\) to \(t+12\)), excluding post-event data, and simulate deployment conditions; then a prospective silent trial.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Discrimination vs calibration for ICU comparison
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. AUROC favours A (0.91 vs 0.88): better discrimination. Average predicted risk favours B for calibration (8.5% vs observed 8%; A predicts 19%, overestimating). In the 30–40% band, A predicts 12% observed (overestimates) while B's 33% is close. So A ranks better, B is calibrated better.
  2. 200 patients × 8% = 16 deaths. Model A predicts 19% × 200 = 38 deaths. O/E = 16/38 ≈ 0.42, suggesting this ICU performs much better than expected — or, more likely, that model A overestimates risk.
  3. Use B (or recalibrate A on held-out data with Platt/isotonic scaling) for O/E comparison, because O/E requires calibration. The table alone cannot establish whether O/E differences reflect quality of care vs case-mix differences (risk adjustment), statistical uncertainty, or subgroup calibration.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Adding X-rays: 0.90 on a selected 1,500
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Not justified. The 0.90 is measured only in the 1,500 patients who had a chest X-ray in the first 24 hours, and those patients have 14% mortality vs 7% overall — a sicker, selected group. The +0.04 cannot be attributed to X-rays for all patients; it is confounded by indication/selection.
  2. At hospital K: no free-text notes, so the notes path is unavailable (structured-only performance, ~0.86 or worse); every ICU patient has an admission X-ray, but the model was trained on selected X-ray patients, so applying the X-ray path to everyone is a different distribution. Expect a performance drop and calibration shift, plus different missing-modality behaviour.
  3. Before use: external validation at K, stratified by available modality, calibration, robustness to missing notes, case-mix comparison, and a prospective silent trial with monitoring.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Age and false-positive rates
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Older patients have higher baseline mortality and comorbidity, so a fixed threshold flags more of them; age is a strong predictor correlated with frailty and atypical presentation. The higher FPR may partly reflect genuine risk, but the disparity is still a fairness problem.
  2. Removing age is unlikely to fix it: the model can reconstruct age from proxies (diagnoses, labs, procedures, notes), so the disparity persists while performance drops and the model becomes less transparent. It treats a symptom, not the cause.
  3. Alternative: subgroup-aware calibration / equalised-odds post-processing, reweighting or more training data for older groups, and auditing subgroup calibration and net benefit. Measure FPR/TPR by group, calibration curves, and clinical net benefit; involve clinicians in setting acceptable trade-offs.

docs.title: Bonus B1 — Random split vs temporal + patient split
docs.text: Answer. Team 2's 0.81 is the better estimate of live performance in 2027. Two separate reasons for the gap: (1) Team 1's random split leaks patients across splits — repeat admissions of the same patient appear in train and test — and ignores time; (2) Team 2's split reflects temporal drift and future deployment, and excludes patients seen in training. Before going live: calibration, subgroup performance, monitoring/drift plan, and consistency of the data pipeline.

docs.title: Bonus B2 — Missing lactate and a new protocol
docs.text:
Answer. The "was measured" feature is a proxy for clinician concern, which is legitimate information available at prediction time — but it is fragile: it encodes a workflow decision, not physiology. After the protocol, lactate is measured for everyone, so the feature becomes constant and loses its predictive power; the lactate distribution also shifts (more normal values), breaking the learned association. Expect miscalibration and a performance drop.

Handling: monitor and retrain/recalibrate after the protocol change, version the model, and replace workflow-artefact features with explicit clinical-concern variables if possible; validate prospectively before relying on it.

docs.title: Problem 1 — Tool description in the prompt
docs.text: Answer. No. Describing the tool only makes the model able to produce a correctly formatted request; it does not establish that the request is executed, that arguments are valid, that the result is parsed and fed back, or that the tool behaves correctly on real inputs. You need an end-to-end test: actual invocation, schema validation, failure/error handling, and evaluation of final outputs against ground truth across representative cases.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Predefined workflow vs agent
docs.text: Answer. Choose the predefined workflow. The possible paths are known in advance: quality fail → replace; incomplete measurements → human review. The deciding question is whether the possible paths can be enumerated, not whether the system branches or uses an LLM. An agent adds non-determinism, cost, latency and validation burden with no benefit when the decision logic is fixed. A workflow with explicit branches and human-review steps is easier to validate, monitor and audit.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Parallelization vs orchestrator-workers
docs.text: Answer. A → predefined parallelization: the three summaries are independent and defined before execution. B → orchestrator-workers: which reviews/analyses are relevant depends on the case, so decomposition must happen at runtime. The architectural difference that matters is whether subtasks are fixed in advance or chosen by the orchestrator. Orchestration adds coordination cost: extra LLM calls and latency, error propagation, non-determinism, harder evaluation, and a synthesizer that must reconcile outputs — justified only when the task genuinely cannot be decomposed in advance.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Evaluator–optimizer criteria
docs.text:
Answer. Direct checks against source records (deterministic): every requested finding present; values and units preserved exactly; chronology/order correct; no fabricated values. Judgement of text (needs a judge): clarity, clinical coherence, no unsupported claims, appropriate emphasis.

Accept only when all deterministic checks pass and the judge scores above a threshold with no new unsupported claims. Use a revision limit as a fallback, but record "revision limit reached" as a failure, distinct from acceptance; log the acceptance reason. Beware evaluator drift and self-preference, so keep a held-out human-rated set to validate the evaluator itself.

docs.title: Problem 5 — AI-SCE-style evaluation of workflow vs agent
docs.text:
Answer. Include situations with missing information, inconsistent records (conflicting medications/labs), ambiguous findings, and routine controls. Record every tool call, query, step taken, tokens/time, and whether missing information was identified and inconsistencies resolved. Compare outcomes (correctness/completeness vs ground truth), process quality (evidence attribution, unnecessary queries, appropriate escalation), and resource use (calls, latency, cost).

To distinguish a well-supported summary from an accidentally correct one: require each statement to cite its source record, score unsupported-but-correct statements as failures, and inject known inconsistencies so you can check detection. Use paired cases and blinded graders.

docs.title: Pattern summary
docs.text: If the question says… Reach for… "lower loss but worse facts" teacher forcing vs generation, loss dominated by common tokens, evaluate the rare critical facts "position added before/after" permutation equivariance; positional info must enter before mixing; averaging destroys order "mask in layer 2 only" leakage through earlier full-attention layer; masking must be causal everywhere "guidelines change / cite the source" RAG + versioned index + citation/abstain, not fine-tuning "per-group vs pooled" stratified metrics, Simpson-style aggregation, subgroup regression "momentum / EMA teacher" stability vs plasticity; slow teacher avoids collapse "frozen probe vs fine-tune" linear separability vs adaptability; a single split cannot establish significance "softmax over descriptions" relative score, not calibrated probability "identical texts in batch" contrastive conflict, multiple positives / dedup "vector length matches" projection + alignment training needed "unseen drug / unperturbed gene" categorical perturbation embedding cannot extrapolate; graph prior transfers "global MSE low" dominated by unchanged genes; evaluate DE genes/deltas "mean of readings" trend information lost; keep slope/min/max "balanced test set, 10% prevalence" PPV = sens·prev / (sens·prev + (1−spec)(1−prev)) "AUROC 0.95 retrospective, 0.71 live" future leakage, not just dataset shift "O/E comparison between ICUs" needs calibration, not just AUROC; risk adjustment "remove age to be fair" proxies remain; subgroup calibration/equalised odds "tool described in prompt" description ≠ execution; end-to-end test "all exceptions known" workflow, not agent "subtasks fixed vs case-dependent" parallelization vs orchestrator-workers

docs.title: Your project · 15%
docs.text:
Poster + code15% of the gradeBe specific

These questions are about your poster and code, so the answers are yours. Below is the shape of a good answer and the terms you must be able to define on the spot.

docs.title: Terms you must know
docs.text: Term Plain meaning Baseline The simplest reference result you must beat (majority class, logistic regression, no-change). Leakage Information in training/test that you would not have at prediction time, or that encodes the answer. Internal validation Held-out data from the same dataset. External validation Data collected independently, another site, period or population. Calibration Predicted risk versus observed risk. Confidence interval A range that expresses uncertainty around an estimate; overlapping intervals mean the difference may be noise. Ablation Remove one component and measure what changes, to show it mattered. Reproducibility Somebody else can rerun your code on the raw inputs and get your numbers.

docs.title: How to answer any project question
docs.text:
1. Claim first. "We tested whether X predicts Y."
  2. Number second. Effect size or metric, with an interval if you have one.
  3. Limitation third. Name it before the examiner does.
  4. Point to the code. "Figure 2 comes from notebook 3, cell 12, seed 42."

Three answers that lose points

"The model is better" with no baseline. "We got 0.9 accuracy" on imbalanced classes. "Random split" without mentioning patient overlap.

docs.title: What is your research question, and which result answers it?
docs.text: Say the population, the input and the outcome in one sentence, then point to the exact panel that tests it. If the question changed during the project, say so and why.

docs.title: Why these data, labels and splits? Where could leakage enter?
