docs.text: Say why the dataset fits the question, how the label was defined, and how the split was made. Then name the concrete leakage risk: same patient on both sides, future data, duplicates, preprocessing fitted on the full set.

docs.title: Why this model and baseline? What would a simpler alternative test?
docs.text: Justify the model by data type and size. Name the baseline and what a simpler model would isolate: is the gain from the architecture or just from more parameters?

docs.title: Which preprocessing and training choices matter most?
docs.text: Pick two or three and say what changes if you flip them: normalisation, class imbalance, augmentation, learning rate, early stopping, seed variance. "We tuned until it worked" is not an answer.

docs.title: What does each metric measure, and what do your numbers establish?
docs.text: Separate discrimination (AUROC) from calibration, and both from the operating point. Say what the number does not establish: one split, one site, no intervals means no claim of significance or transportability.

docs.title: How does the code reproduce each figure and table?
docs.text: For each panel: input file, script or notebook, command, output. Mention the environment, seeds and any manual step. If something is not reproducible, say it — that is a limitation, not a disqualification.

docs.title: Where does your approach fail, and what would you test next?
docs.text:
Name the main failure mode, the strongest limitation (data, labels, evaluation, compute), and the one next experiment that would be decisive. An honest limitation scores better than a confident overclaim.

If you remember one thing

Every poster claim should survive: "compared to what, measured how, on whom?"

docs.title: 2 · Vision models
docs.text:
Lecture 2~15 minRead → answer → check

How an image becomes a vector, and the three tricks used to make that vector useful: self-supervision, contrastive learning, and generative vision–language models.

docs.title: 1. An image becomes a vector
docs.text:
Explanation. An encoder is a neural network that turns an image into a fixed-length vector, called a feature or embedding. "Frozen" means the encoder's weights are not changed during your task. A classifier on top then maps the vector to a label.

Term. Linear probe: a single layer \(p = \mathrm{softmax}(Wz+b)\) trained on fixed features \(z\). Fine-tuning updates the encoder itself.

Check yourself

Encoder A gets 78% with a frozen linear probe and 86% fine-tuned; B gets 84% and 85%. Which encoder do you pick in each case, and what does the table not prove?

Answer

Frozen: B (84 > 78). Fine-tuned: A (86 > 85). A probe measures only how linearly separable the existing features are; fine-tuning can reshape them, so A may be less linearly accessible but more adaptable. The table does not establish significance (one split, no intervals), external validity, overfitting, or cost — a one-point gap is within noise.

docs.title: 2. Self-supervised learning makes its own labels
docs.text:
Explanation. Self-supervised means the supervision comes from the data itself, not from annotators. One recipe: take two augmented views of the same image (crop, colour jitter, blur), and train the model to give them similar representations. It learns invariance — the representation ignores changes that do not change the content.

Check yourself

Why do two different views of the same image help a model learn without labels, and what can augmentation accidentally destroy?

Answer

The two views are related observations of the same content, so forcing consistent representations teaches invariance to irrelevant changes. Aggressive augmentation can destroy clinically meaningful detail (a small lesion cropped away), which is why medical self-supervision uses gentler transforms.

docs.title: 3. DINO: a student learns from a slow teacher
docs.text:
Explanation. DINO passes two views through a student network and a teacher network. The teacher's output is the target; the student is trained to match it. The teacher's weights are an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student's: $ \theta_\text{teacher} \leftarrow m\,\theta_\text{teacher} + (1-m)\,\theta_\text{student}$. The momentum \(m\) controls how slowly the teacher changes.

Check yourself

Compare \(m = 0\), \(0.9\), \(0.999\) and \(1\). Why does a slowly changing teacher help?

Answer

\(m=0\): teacher = student, the target moves every step and training can oscillate or collapse. \(0.9\): memory of ~10 steps, only mild stability. \(0.999\): memory of ~1000 steps, stable targets that prevent collapse — the useful regime. \(m=1\): frozen random teacher, stable but useless because the student learns meaningless initial features. A slow teacher acts like an ensemble of past students, giving low-variance targets.

docs.title: 4. Collapse: when all images look the same
docs.text:
Explanation. A trivial way to make two views similar is to output the same vector for every image — representation collapse. DINO avoids it with centring (subtract the batch mean from the teacher's outputs, so no single dimension dominates) and sharpening (divide the logits by a small temperature, making the target distribution confident); DINOv2 adds a feature-spread regulariser that pushes features apart (prevents dimensional collapse, where features crowd into a narrow subspace).

Check yourself

Remove the spread regulariser. What goes wrong, and which measurements would reveal it?

Answer

Features crowd into a narrow region: neighbours become uninformative and patch features lose the diversity needed for segmentation, even if total collapse is avoided. Reveal it with the effective rank of the feature matrix, pairwise and kNN distance distributions, linear-probe accuracy, patch-level probes and clustering quality — the matching loss alone can look fine.

docs.title: 5. CLIP: match images with text
docs.text:
Explanation. CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together. For a batch of \(N\) image–text pairs it maximises the similarity of the \(N\) correct pairs and minimises the \(N^2-N\) wrong ones — a contrastive objective. Afterwards, zero-shot classification compares an image with the embeddings of candidate text prompts.

Check yourself

A batch contains two different images paired with the same caption. Can each image put all probability on its own copy, and how do you fix it?

Answer

No. Both texts are identical, so their similarities to a given image are equal; the softmax cannot give all mass to one copy and none to the other, and the gradients conflict. Fix by deduplicating the batch, ensuring unique texts, or using a multiple-positive contrastive loss that treats all identical texts as positives.

docs.title: 6. A softmax over prompts is not a probability
docs.text:
Explanation. CLIP computes a similarity for each candidate prompt and applies softmax over that candidate set. Adding a prompt changes the denominator, so every score changes even if the image is untouched. The output is a relative ranking among the prompts you wrote, not a calibrated disease probability.

Check yourself

"Abnormal" scores 0.90 against two prompts. You add a third prompt, "pneumonia", without changing the image. Can the 0.90 change, and is it a 90% chance of disease?

Answer

Yes, it can change: softmax normalises across the candidate set, so a new option takes probability mass from the others. And no — 0.90 is a relative score within that prompt list. A real probability needs calibration on held-out data with a fixed, clinically defined set of classes.

docs.title: 7. Vision–language models need a projection
docs.text:
Explanation. A VLM such as LLaVA feeds image features into a language model. Vector lengths may match, but the two spaces have different scales and geometry. A learned projection maps image features into the language model's embedding space, and alignment/instruction tuning teaches the model to use those visual tokens (usually several tokens, not one).

Check yourself

A frozen CLIP vector has exactly the same dimension as the LLM's token embeddings. Can you feed it in directly?

Answer

No. Same length does not mean same space; the CLIP vector is out of distribution for the LLM, which has never learned to interpret it. You need a trained projection plus alignment training, or the model ignores or misreads the image.

docs.title: 8. Retrieval versus generation
docs.text:
Explanation. Retrieval selects an existing report from a database by similarity. Generation predicts a new sequence of tokens. Retrieval is grounded and cannot hallucinate a new finding, but it can only reuse what exists; generation is flexible but can fabricate.

Check yourself

For an archive with 200,000 prior reports, which approach would you choose for a first draft, and what is its main failure mode?

Answer

Retrieval: it selects the most similar existing report, so it cannot invent findings, but it can return a report about a different patient or an outdated style/content that does not fit. Generation is more flexible but can hallucinate.

docs.title: 9. Validation decides whether it works
docs.text:
Explanation. Internal validation holds out part of the same dataset. External validation uses independently collected data from another site, scanner or period. Only external validation tests whether the model transports.

Check yourself

A model has AUROC 0.97 on a random 20% split of one hospital's data. What has been established?

Answer

Internal performance on that hospital's data distribution. Nothing about other scanners, populations or time periods; the split may even leak patients. Transportability requires external validation and, for deployment, local calibration.

If you remember one thing

A CLIP score is a ranking among the prompts you typed, never a disease probability.

docs.title: Clinical workflow cases · worked answers
docs.text:
Lecture 58 deployment casesThe 50% part

The eight guided self-study cases from "Integration of AI in the clinical workflow". Each answer follows the required structure: the decision, the number that drove it, the risk you cannot mitigate, and who owns that risk.

Exam move

For any deployment scenario, answer in this order: intended use → unit of output → validation → operating point → monitoring/exit plan → economics. Most lost points come from jumping to AUROC before asking whether the use is even inside the intended use.

docs.title: Case 1 — Melanoma model meets dermatopathology
docs.text:
Published research model, AUROC 0.96 on 1,200 curated balanced slides from one scanner; web app; 14,000 skin specimens/year; melanocytic lesions 18%, re-excisions 7%.

Scope. Melanocytic lesions: \(0.18 \times 14{,}000 = 2{,}520\) specimens/year, and at ~3 slides each ≈ 7,560 slides/year. The other 82% (BCC, SCC/AK, seborrhoeic keratosis, inflammatory, re-excisions, other) are out of scope: the model has no validated output for them. Routing is decided at accessioning/triage by the lab, not by the model.

Unit of output. One probability per slide is not a diagnosis. The report needs: lesion classification with subtype, Bresenham thickness, ulceration, mitotic rate, margin status (peripheral/deep), lymphovascular invasion, regression, and a case-level integrated diagnosis across slides. The model gives none of these, and no uncertainty or evidence per feature.

Allowed? No, as it stands. Governance problems: (1) it is a research prototype, not CE-IVD/MDR-certified, with no intended-use statement; (2) sending patient slides to an external university web app needs a data-processing agreement, GDPR basis, and security review; (3) no local validation on your scanner, population and case mix; (4) no accreditation/quality system, monitoring or liability agreement. Local validation alone would not fix the regulatory status.

docs.title: Case 2 — One prostate model, three proposals
docs.text:
CE-IVD, intended use: adjunct, pathologist reviews all slides. 12 cores on 6 slides, 3-week backlog.

  • A — worklist prioritisation: inside intended use. Every case is still read; this only changes order. Validation duty: show that prioritisation does not delay the rest beyond an acceptable bound.
  • B — in-viewer overlay: inside intended use (adjunct, pathologist reviews everything). Validation: overlay does not cause misses/automation bias.
  • C — "AI benign" fast track: outside intended use. It converts an adjunct into a rule-out/sign-out tool, which is a new clinical claim: new validation, potentially new regulatory status, and new liability. It also requires a case-level operating point and a documented policy for who signs out.

Aggregation. For A, use the maximum slide score per case — you want suspicious cases first, so any positive core should raise the case. For C, the case is "AI benign" only if every slide (and every core) has \(p < \tau\), i.e. the case score is the max; using the mean would dilute one positive core and destroy case-level sensitivity.

Tomorrow's choice. Take A, with one condition: a prospective audit of time-to-read for high-score cases and a monthly review of misses in the prioritised list; no case may be delayed beyond the agreed window.

docs.title: Case 3 — Choose the operating point
docs.text:
10,000 node slides/year (250 working days = 40/day), 5% metastasis → 500 positive, 9,500 negative.

Sens Spec TP FP FN TN PPV NPV Flags/day A 0.99 0.70 495 2,850 5 6,650 14.8% 99.92% 13.4 B 0.95 0.90 475 950 25 8,550 33.3% 99.71% 5.7 C 0.85 0.98 425 190 75 9,310 69.1% 99.20% 2.5

Worked (A): TP = 0.99×500 = 495; FN = 5; FP = 0.30×9,500 = 2,850; PPV = 495/(495+2,850); NPV = 6,650/6,655.

Assistant (i): choose A. The pathologist reads every slide anyway, so a false positive costs a few seconds of extra review, while a false negative is a missed metastasis. Sensitivity dominates.

Rule-out (ii): the model-negative slides are seen by no human, so the FN count is the harm: A = 5, B = 25, C = 75 missed metastases/year. Workload removed: A 6,650 (66.5%), B 8,550 (85.5%), C 9,310 (93.1%). Choose A or B depending on the explicitly accepted miss rate; C is only defensible if local validation shows a clinically acceptable NPV and the lab accepts ~75 unseen metastases/year.

Why AUROC is useless here. AUROC integrates over all thresholds and is prevalence-independent; it does not tell you the FP/FN trade-off at a specific operating point, which is the entire decision. The threshold is a clinical risk decision: the clinical lead/pathologist with lab management and quality/regulatory sign-off, not the vendor or IT.

docs.title: Case 4 — The CE mark is not the end of the story
docs.text:
PD-L1 TPS, cut-offs 1% and 50%; vendor: 3 centres, 600 cases, ICC 0.90. Your lab: different antibody (SP263 vs 22C3), stainer, scanner, and cytology cell blocks.

Inside intended use? Antibody, stainer, scanner and specimen type all differ. Some differences may be covered by the vendor's validation; cytology cell blocks likely are not. Anything outside the intended use is your validation responsibility, and off-label use is the lab's liability.

Why ICC 0.90 is the wrong metric. ICC measures agreement on the continuous score across all values; it can be high while agreement at the clinically decisive cut-offs (1%, 50%) is poor. What matters is categorical agreement at the thresholds: accuracy/agreement, kappa, sensitivity/specificity for "≥1%" and "≥50%", with confidence intervals, plus a Bland–Altman plot focused near the cut-offs.

Site validation. ≥60 consecutive routine cases per application (CAP/ASCP/API 2022), enriched near the cut-offs, including cytology cell blocks. Reference standard: consensus of ≥3 pathologists (adjudication), not a single sign-out. Metrics: categorical agreement at 1% and 50% with CIs, plus directional bias. Pre-specify acceptance (e.g. lower CI bound of agreement ≥90%, no systematic shift).

Ground truth. There is no perfect truth near the cut-offs. Build a consensus panel with adjudication, blinded to AI, and where available use clinical outcome/response as an anchor. Report disagreement explicitly rather than pretending the sign-out is truth.

docs.title: Case 5 — HER2 drift
docs.text:
Validation combined 0 and 1+ as "negative". M4: post-neoadjuvant resections 5% → 20%. M6: HER2-low therapy makes 0 vs 1+ decisive. No error was ever raised.

  1. Patients or model? Both are plausible: post-neoadjuvant residual disease genuinely has different HER2 distributions (more 0/1+), and the model may drift with a new case mix/staining. To separate: pull case mix by indication and specimen type, scanner/stainer changes, the AI score distribution within the same subgroup, pathologist–AI agreement over time, override reasons, and re-review a sample of 0/1+ cases. If the shift disappears within matched subgroups, it is patients; if not, suspect the model.
  2. What is the old validation worth? Near zero for the new decision: it never measured 0 vs 1+ discrimination, only negative vs positive. No dashboard changes because the model output and thresholds did not change — the clinical meaning of the boundary changed, which no monitoring metric watches.
  3. New validation: enrich 0/1+ cases, consensus reference standard, metric = agreement/accuracy between 0 and 1+ at the therapy decision, pre-specified acceptance; include post-neoadjuvant cases.
  4. Who is harmed: HER2-low patients misclassified 1+→0 are denied therapy; 0→1+ may be given an inappropriate option. Rough size: at 1,500 breast cancers/year, the 0 share rose ~10 points (25→35%) and 1+ fell ~8 points; if even half of that shift is misclassification, ~60–100 patients/year are affected.

docs.title: Case 6 — The model that cannot be proven wrong
docs.text:
Zero discrepancies among "not needed" cases; vendor claims NPV 100%.

  1. Why not evidence. Only cases where IHC was not ordered were audited, and the final report is produced by the same pathologist who saw the AI suggestion (anchoring). No case has a reference standard that could reveal a missed diagnosis, so true false negatives were never measured. "Zero discrepancies" means "nobody looked for a disagreement".
  2. Design. Randomise cases near the decision boundary to IHC vs no IHC (MASAI-style), or use held-out periods; sample a random fraction of "not needed" cases for IHC and compare AI-suggested vs IHC-supported diagnosis; log the AI output and the clinical action separately; pre-register a non-inferiority margin and a safety endpoint (missed clinically significant cancers).
  3. Ethics. Doing IHC on tissue already taken is minimal risk and low cost, and there is genuine equipoise near the boundary. Answer the committee with: minimal incremental risk, clinical equipoise, opt-out/waiver, independent oversight, pre-specified stopping rules, and the fact that the current "100% NPV" claim is itself an unvalidated clinical claim.

docs.title: Case 7 — Faster, cheaper, nobody disagrees
docs.text:
Chest X-ray assistant; −22% reporting time; agreement 91% → 98.6%; senior stopped using it; juniors unsure during an outage.

  1. What does 98.6% mean? Not necessarily quality. Rising agreement is consistent with automation bias (readers defer to the AI), not calibrated trust. Data that distinguish: blinded independent reads, audits on a sample including AI-error cases, accuracy before vs after deployment, override outcomes in both directions, and whether readers detect deliberately inserted AI errors.
  2. Reverse-centaur symptoms: raising the daily target 20% (speed over judgement), requiring written justification to disagree (punishes override), reporting override rate with the aim to reduce it (treats disagreement as error), making it mandatory for everyone (removes the centaur's choice). Rewrite: AI as second reader/prioritisation, no target increase, disagreement logged without justification, override rate reviewed for both directions, opt-out allowed.
  3. Interface. Show the output after the initial read or on demand, show the image with regions rather than a single number, make dismissal one click and logged. Replace "confidence 94%" with a calibrated risk statement ("no nodule detected; sensitivity for nodules ≥8 mm is X%") or a risk band validated on local data.
  4. Legal. The radiologist who overrode with documented justification is better protected: the record shows independent judgement. Following the AI is not a defence. Designing policy that punishes override therefore increases automation bias.

docs.title: Case 8 — Business case
docs.text:
1,800 cases/year; licence €25/case; IHC in 30% of cases at €60; 40% relative IHC reduction; 12 min/case at €150/h; 20% time saving; validation 0.1 FTE; integration €40,000.

  • Licence: \(1{,}800 \times 25 = €45{,}000\)/year.
  • IHC saved: \(0.30 \times 1{,}800 \times 0.40 = 216\) cases \(\times 60 = €12{,}960\)/year.
  • Time saved: \(1{,}800 \times 12/60 = 360\) h; 20% = 72 h \(\times 150 = €10{,}800\)/year.
  • Validation: 0.1 FTE — at ~€200k loaded cost ≈ €20,000/year (state the assumption).
  • Year 1: \(12{,}960 + 10{,}800 - 45{,}000 - 20{,}000 - 40{,}000 = \mathbf{-€81{,}240}\). Steady state ≈ −€41,240/year.

So it does not pay for itself on IHC and reading time alone. It only works if freed capacity is converted into something: filling the two vacancies, avoiding locum/temporary staff, or additional throughput.

Fractional and distributed benefits: minutes saved per case, turnaround improvement, consistency. The finance director's question "which cost disappears?" has only two honest answers: IHC consumables (€12,960) and avoided locum/overtime or avoided hiring. Everything else is capacity, not cash.

Who pays / captures: the lab pays the licence, integration and validation; the insurer pays the bundled tariff; urology and patients capture faster turnaround. The bundled tariff means efficiency gains do not become revenue — the lab bears the cost and the benefit is captured elsewhere. That is the core argument for a separate funding or shared-savings arrangement.

Non-financial case: two unfilled pathologist posts, three-week backlog, urology complaints, recruitment and sub-specialisation. Evidence needed: locally validated non-inferiority, measured time saving, backlog/turnaround reduction, and staff acceptance.

docs.title: Closing questions
docs.text:
• AUROC changed the decision in almost none of the cases. The cases were decided by intended use, unit of output, operating point, drift, human factors and economics.
  • The recurring risk owner is the clinical lead / responsible pathologist or radiologist, usually not in the room when the model is bought.
  • The framework question that would have prevented most problems: Q8 (how will it be used in practice?) and Q9 (what could go wrong?), asked before purchase.

docs.title: 5 · Clinical workflow integration
docs.text:
Lecture 5~25 minThe 50% part

A good model is not a good product. This page defines the vocabulary of deployment, one decision at a time, with a question after each.

docs.title: 1. Intended use is the first question
docs.text:
Explanation. Intended use is the formal statement of what a device is for: which patients, which decision, and whether a human decides. CE-IVD (in-vitro diagnostic) is the European mark that a product may be sold for a stated clinical use. Adjunct means the clinician reviews everything anyway; triage only changes the order; rule-out means a negative result may skip a human read; QC checks that the sample or slide is usable.

Check yourself

A melanoma model is validated on 1,200 curated slides and offered for 14,000 mixed skin specimens/year. Which specimens are in scope, and what is missing from its output?

Answer

Only melanocytic lesions: 18% × 14,000 = 2,520 specimens/year, at ~3 slides each ≈ 7,560 slides; the other 82% have no validated output. The output is one probability per slide, but a report needs subtype, Bresenham thickness, ulceration, mitotic rate, margins, lymphovascular invasion, regression, and a case-level conclusion — none of which it provides, nor uncertainty.

docs.title: 2. Four integration patterns
docs.text:
Explanation. Where the model sits relative to the human decides its failure mode:

Pattern The model acts Main failure mode Example Triage / pre-screen Before the human, reorders the queue Delay (a missed case is still read) Worklist prioritisation Concurrent assistant Alongside the human, in the viewer Automation bias, anchoring Overlay during reading Second reader / QC After the human, flags discrepancies Alert fatigue, over-calling Report discrepancy checking Autonomous Instead of the human Undetected error reaches the patient Retinal screening

Validation depth, regulatory burden and liability all increase as you move down the table.

Human in vs on the loop. In the loop: every output passes through a human — risk is automation bias, and the human must keep the unassisted skill. On the loop: the system acts and the human monitors — risk is vigilance decrement, because monitoring a reliable system is something humans are bad at.

Check yourself

A model is sold as an autonomous retinal screener and deployed in primary care where no ophthalmologist is present. Who is accountable, and what must the validation show?

Answer

Arguably the manufacturer, because the primary-care physician cannot independently judge a retinal image and should not carry the liability. Validation must be prospective and site-specific, at the operating point used, with a defined escalation path and drift monitoring; autonomous use needs the deepest evidence, not the shallowest.

docs.title: 3. The output unit decides the aggregation
docs.text:
Explanation. The unit of output is what the score refers to: a slide, a case (several slides/cores), or a patient. If the decision is case-level, you must aggregate slide scores. For triage, use the maximum slide score per case — any suspicious slide should raise the case. For a rule-out, the case is negative only if every slide is below the threshold, which is also the maximum rule.

Check yourself

A prostate case has 12 cores on 6 slides. The model outputs a probability per slide. How do you turn this into a case decision for triage, and why not use the mean?

Answer

Use the maximum slide probability: suspicious cases go first, so one positive core should raise the case. The mean would dilute a single positive core across many negative slides and could hide exactly the case that needs attention.

docs.title: 4. The operating point is a clinical decision
docs.text:
Explanation. The operating point is the threshold that turns a score into an action. Lowering it catches more positives (higher sensitivity) but flags more negatives (lower specificity, lower PPV, more workload). PPV and NPV at that threshold depend on prevalence. AUROC summarizes all thresholds and therefore does not choose one.

Papers report AUROC and balanced accuracy; deployment needs sensitivity/specificity at the shipped threshold, PPV/NPV at the true prevalence, patient-level outcomes (not slide-level), worst-subgroup performance, and operational endpoints (turnaround time, override rate, interval cancers).

Check yourself

10,000 slides/year (40/day), 5% prevalence. A: sens 0.99, spec 0.70. B: sens 0.95, spec 0.90. C: sens 0.85, spec 0.98. Compute PPV and missed positives (FN) for A and C, then choose for (i) an assistant where every slide is read, and (ii) a rule-out where negatives are not read.

Answer

A: TP 495, FN 5, FP 2,850, PPV = 495/3,345 ≈ 14.8%, NPV 99.92%. C: TP 425, FN 75, FP 190, PPV = 425/615 ≈ 69.1%, NPV 99.20%. (i) Assistant → A: a false positive costs seconds, a false negative is a missed metastasis. (ii) Rule-out → A or B; the harm is the FN count (A 5, B 25, C 75 per year), so C is defensible only if the lab accepts ~75 unseen metastases. Threshold: clinical lead with lab management and quality sign-off.

docs.title: 5. A CE mark covers only the validated use
docs.text:
Explanation. A cut-off is the value of a biomarker that separates categories (e.g. PD-L1 at 1% and 50%). ICC (intraclass correlation) measures agreement on a continuous score across its whole range. Categorical agreement measures agreement at the clinically decisive cut-offs. Validation must use a reference standard independent of the model — usually a consensus of several pathologists.

Check yourself

A PD-L1 model is CE-IVD with ICC 0.90, but your lab uses a different antibody, stainer, scanner and cytology cell blocks. What must you validate, with what metric and reference standard?

Answer

Anything outside the vendor's intended use is your responsibility: antibody, stainer, scanner and cytology blocks. ICC 0.90 is the wrong metric because it can hide poor agreement at the cut-offs; report categorical agreement at 1% and 50% (accuracy, kappa, sensitivity/specificity with confidence intervals) plus a Bland–Altman plot near the thresholds. Use ≥60 consecutive routine cases per application, enriched near the cut-offs; reference standard = consensus of ≥3 pathologists blinded to AI, not a single sign-out.

Four kinds of validation. Internal: held-out split from the same source — did it learn the training distribution? External: an independent cohort from another centre/scanner — does it transfer? Prospective: consecutive, unselected, real-time cases — does it work on tomorrow's patients? Site-specific clinical: local cases on local equipment before go-live. Professional guidance (CAP/ASCP/API 2022) is explicit: validation should emulate the lab's real environment, with at least 60 routine cases per application.

Check yourself

A paper reports internal validation 0.94 and external 0.81. Which number would you quote to the lab that is buying it, and what is still missing?

Answer

The external 0.81 is the better estimate of transport, but even that is not the local number. Still missing: site-specific validation on the lab's scanner, stainer and case mix, plus prospective consecutive cases, calibration, and a monitoring/exit plan.

docs.title: 6. Monitoring exists to catch drift — including meaning drift
docs.text:
Explanation. Drift is a change in the data distribution or in the relationship between score and outcome. Monitoring watches inputs, score distributions, and outcomes. But a change in clinical meaning (a new therapy makes 0 versus 1+ decisive) can occur with no change in the model or its numbers, so no dashboard fires.

Mechanism Cause Detectable by Covariate shift New scanner, stainer, protocol, reagent lot Input statistics (stain vectors, focus scores) Label / prior shift Case mix or referral pattern changes Output distribution vs baseline Concept drift A guideline changes what the label means Only by human audit Feedback loop The model influences the labels it is later trained on Very hard

The silent failure: none of these produce an error message; the model keeps returning confident, plausible output.

Check yourself

A HER2 model was validated treating 0 and 1+ as "negative". Case mix changes and a HER2-low therapy makes 0 versus 1+ decisive. Is the old validation still worth anything, and what do you do?

Answer

Almost nothing: it measured negative versus positive, never 0 versus 1+. Nothing flags it because the model output and thresholds did not change — only what the boundary means. Revalidate by enriching 0/1+ cases (including post-neoadjuvant), using a consensus reference standard, measuring agreement between 0 and 1+ at the therapy decision, and pre-specifying acceptance. Meanwhile, compare score distributions within matched subgroups to separate patient change from model drift.

docs.title: 7. Human factors: agreement is not accuracy
docs.text:
Explanation. Automation bias is the tendency to accept a machine's suggestion, especially when it is usually right. Override is a clinician rejecting the model. A rising agreement rate can mean better quality — or that people stopped checking.

Check yourself

Agreement rises from 91% to 98.6%, reporting time falls 22%, seniors stop using the system and juniors are lost during an outage. Does this prove benefit?

Answer

No. Rising agreement is consistent with automation bias, not calibrated trust. Distinguish with blinded independent reads, audits that include AI-error cases, accuracy before versus after, override outcomes in both directions, and deliberately inserted errors. Redesign: AI as second reader or prioritisation, no speed target, one-click logged dismissal, output after the first read, calibrated risk statements, and an opt-out.

docs.title: 8. The business case: minutes are not cash
docs.text:
Explanation. FTE = full-time equivalent, a person's annual working time (loaded cost ≈ €200k in this case). Tariff = the fixed price paid for a procedure. Saved clinician minutes are capacity, not money, unless they are converted into something (filling a vacancy, avoiding a locum) or the tariff is paid per case.

Check yourself

1,800 cases/year; licence €25/case; IHC in 30% at €60, 40% relative reduction; 12 min/case at €150/h, 20% saved; validation 0.1 FTE; integration €40,000. Does it pay for itself in year 1?

Answer

Licence €45,000. IHC saved: 0.30 × 1,800 × 0.40 = 216 cases × €60 = €12,960. Time saved: 1,800 × 0.2 h = 360 h, 20% = 72 h × €150 = €10,800. Validation ≈ €20,000. Year 1: 12,960 + 10,800 − 45,000 − 20,000 − 40,000 = −€81,240 (steady state ≈ −€41,240). It does not pay for itself unless freed capacity becomes cash — filling two vacancies or avoiding locums. The lab pays; the insurer pays the bundled tariff; urology and patients capture the faster turnaround.

docs.title: 9. The model that cannot be proven wrong
docs.text:
Explanation. A reference standard is the best available truth. If only cases where the model said "not needed" are audited without doing the test, no false negative can ever be found — verification bias. The prediction paradox: acting on a prediction destroys the evidence needed to check it.

Check yourself

A vendor reports zero discrepancies among cases where IHC was "not needed" and claims 100% NPV. Why is this not evidence, and how would you design a real evaluation?

Answer

Only cases where IHC was not ordered were audited, and the pathologist saw the AI suggestion (anchoring); no reference standard could reveal a missed diagnosis, so false negatives were never measured. Design: randomise boundary cases to IHC versus no IHC (MASAI-style), or send a random sample of "not needed" cases to IHC; log AI output and clinical action separately; pre-register a non-inferiority margin and a safety endpoint (missed significant cancers). Ethically it is minimal risk because tissue is already taken.

If you remember one thing

For any deployment question: intended use → unit of output → validation → operating point → monitoring → economics, then name who owns the residual risk.
